options.text: is lost as heat and never returns

items.stem: Name the two components of an ecosystem.
items.answer: The biotic component, consisting of all the living organisms, namely producers, consumers and decomposers; and the abiotic component, consisting of the non-living surroundings such as air, water, soil, light and temperature.

items.stem: Name the four kinds of consumer with an example of each.
items.answer: Herbivores, which eat plants, such as a cow; carnivores, which eat other animals, such as a lion; omnivores, which eat both, such as a human being; and parasites, which take nourishment from a living host, such as a tapeworm.

items.stem: Why are non-biodegradable substances a problem?
items.answer: Micro-organisms cannot break them down, so they persist in the environment for decades or centuries. They accumulate, clog drains and soil, and if they are toxic they pass up food chains and become concentrated in the animals at the top.

items.stem: Why is the ozone layer important to life on Earth?
items.answer: It absorbs most of the harmful ultraviolet radiation from the sun. Without it, that radiation would reach the surface and cause skin cancer, cataracts and damage to crops and to the plankton on which ocean food chains depend.

items.stem: Why are food chains usually limited to three or four steps?
items.answer: Because only about ten per cent of the energy passes from one level to the next, the energy available falls very steeply. After three or four transfers too little remains to support another level of consumers.

items.stem: What are the three Rs of waste management?
items.answer: Reduce, meaning use less in the first place; reuse, meaning use an article again rather than discarding it; and recycle, meaning process the material into something new. Reduce is the most effective of the three, since waste that is never created needs no handling.

items.stem: Explain why biological magnification affects human beings so strongly.
items.answer: Human beings are omnivores who often feed at the top of several food chains, eating both plants and animals including fish and meat. Non-biodegradable toxins concentrate at every transfer, so consuming organisms from high trophic levels delivers the accumulated burden of all the levels beneath them.

items.stem: Why is matter recycled in an ecosystem while energy is not?
items.answer: Matter is conserved and can pass repeatedly between organisms and the environment, so decomposers return the same atoms to the soil for reuse. Energy is degraded to heat at every transfer and that heat disperses into space, so it cannot be recovered and must be continually resupplied by the sun.

items.stem: Describe the components of an ecosystem and explain how they interact.
items.answer: An ecosystem has two components. The abiotic component consists of the non-living physical surroundings: air, water, soil, sunlight, temperature and minerals. The biotic component consists of all the living organisms, and these fall into three functional groups. Producers, which are the green plants and blue-green algae, use sunlight, carbon dioxide and water to make their own food by photosynthesis, and they are the only entry point for energy into the system. Consumers depend on food made by others, and are classified as herbivores, carnivores, omnivores and parasites. Decomposers, which are the bacteria and fungi, break down the dead remains and wastes of the other two groups. The interaction runs as follows. Energy enters as sunlight and is captured by the producers, then passes to consumers as they feed, losing about ninety per cent at each transfer as heat. Matter follows the same route but does not stop there: decomposers release the nutrients locked in dead bodies back into the soil and air, where the producers absorb them again. So energy flows through the ecosystem in one direction and is lost, while matter cycles round it repeatedly, and the abiotic component is both the source of that matter and the medium in which everything takes place.

items.stem: Explain what a food chain is, and give one terrestrial and one aquatic example with trophic levels marked.
items.answer: A food chain is a series of organisms in which each feeds on the one before it, so that food and the energy it contains are transferred step by step. Each step is called a trophic level. A terrestrial example is grass, then grasshopper, then frog, then snake, then hawk. Here grass is the producer at the first trophic level; the grasshopper is the primary consumer, a herbivore, at the second; the frog is the secondary consumer at the third; the snake is the tertiary consumer at the fourth; and the hawk is the quaternary consumer at the fifth. An aquatic example is phytoplankton, then zooplankton, then small fish, then large fish. Phytoplankton are the producers, zooplankton the primary consumers, small fish the secondary consumers and large fish the tertiary consumers. In both cases the number of organisms and the total energy fall sharply at each step, which is why the chains are short. Decomposers are not usually numbered as a trophic level because they act on dead material from every level rather than occupying one position in the sequence.

items.stem: State the ten percent law and explain what happens to the energy that is not transferred.
items.answer: The ten percent law states that when energy passes from one trophic level to the next, only about ten per cent of it is stored in the body of the organism at the higher level and becomes available to the level above, while about ninety per cent is lost. The energy is not destroyed; it goes to four places. A large part is used by the organism in respiration to power its own life processes, and that energy ultimately appears as heat. Some is lost directly as heat to the surroundings from the body. Some is contained in food that is eaten but not digested, and leaves the body in the faeces. And some is simply never eaten at all, remaining in parts of the organism the consumer does not take, or in individuals that die and pass instead to the decomposers. Because the loss compounds at each step, the consequences are large: of 10000 units captured by plants, about 1000 reach herbivores, about 100 the next level and about 10 the level above that. This is why food chains rarely exceed four or five steps, why the number and total mass of organisms decreases up a chain, and why a given area of land can feed far more people on a vegetarian diet than on a meat diet.

items.stem: Explain how ozone is formed, how it is depleted, and what has been done about it.
items.answer: Ozone is formed high in the atmosphere when ultraviolet radiation from the sun splits ordinary oxygen molecules into free oxygen atoms, and these atoms combine with other oxygen molecules to give ozone, which has three atoms. The process is continuous, and a steady amount of ozone is maintained high in the stratosphere. Its importance is that it absorbs most of the harmful ultraviolet radiation, preventing it from reaching the surface. Depletion is caused chiefly by chlorofluorocarbons, synthetic chemicals that were widely used as refrigerants and in aerosol sprays. They are extremely stable, so they drift up to the stratosphere unchanged, where ultraviolet light breaks them apart and releases chlorine atoms. A single chlorine atom can destroy a great many ozone molecules in a chain of reactions before it is removed, which is why small quantities of these chemicals have a large effect. A sharp drop in ozone over Antarctica was detected in 1985 and became known as the ozone hole. The response was international. In 1987 an agreement known as the Montreal Protocol was adopted, under which the manufacture and use of these chemicals was frozen and then phased out. Manufacturers moved to alternative refrigerants, and the measure is generally regarded as a success, though because the chemicals already released persist for decades the layer is expected to take most of this century to recover.

items.stem: Describe the main methods of waste disposal and assess the drawbacks of each.
items.answer: Landfill involves burying waste in low-lying land and covering it with soil. It is cheap and handles large volumes, but it consumes land, and liquid draining from the site can contaminate groundwater, while decomposing organic matter releases methane. Incineration burns waste at high temperature, greatly reducing its volume and allowing energy recovery, but it produces ash and releases pollutants including toxic gases unless the flue gases are carefully treated, and the plants are expensive. Composting converts biodegradable waste into manure by microbial action, which is inexpensive and returns nutrients to the soil, but it works only for biodegradable material and needs the waste to be segregated first. Recycling processes materials such as paper, glass, metal and some plastics into new products, saving raw material and energy, but it requires collection and sorting, some materials degrade with each cycle, and the process itself uses energy and water. Sewage treatment deals with liquid waste through settling, biological digestion and disinfection before discharge, but plants are costly and are often inadequate for the volumes produced. The assessment worth making is that none of these methods is a solution on its own, since each moves the problem rather than removing it. This is why the three Rs place reduce first: waste that is never generated needs no disposal, and segregation at source is what makes every one of the other methods work better.

items.stem: Explain biological magnification with a worked illustration, and state why it is dangerous.
items.answer: Biological magnification is the progressive increase in the concentration of a non-biodegradable substance at successive trophic levels of a food chain. The cause is that such a substance is neither broken down nor excreted, so it is retained in the body of the organism that takes it in. Since a consumer eats many individuals of the level below, it accumulates the burden of all of them, while its own body mass is much smaller than their total. To illustrate, suppose water contains a pesticide at 0.003 parts per million. Plankton absorbing it directly may hold 0.04 ppm. Small fish eating large numbers of plankton reach perhaps 0.5 ppm. Larger fish eating those reach perhaps 2 ppm. A fish-eating bird at the top may reach 25 ppm, thousands of times the concentration in the water. The danger has several parts. The concentration in the top consumer can reach a level that is toxic even though the concentration in the environment is far too low to harm anything directly, so the water may appear safe by measurement while the food chain is not. The organisms most affected are the top predators, which are usually the least numerous and slowest to breed, so populations can collapse. Human beings are particularly exposed because we are omnivores who eat from the top of several chains, including fish and meat. And the effect is delayed and cumulative, so damage appears long after the chemical was used, by which time it is widely distributed and cannot be recalled. This is why pesticides such as DDT were restricted, and why persistence in the environment is now treated as a hazard in its own right, separate from immediate toxicity.

items.stem: Explain why the number and total mass of organisms usually decrease at each higher trophic level.
items.answer: The explanation lies in the ten percent law. Only about a tenth of the energy at one trophic level is stored in the bodies of the organisms at the next, the remaining nine tenths being used in respiration, lost as heat, passed out undigested or never eaten. Since the energy available to a level sets a limit on the total living matter it can support, that total mass must fall by roughly a factor of ten at each step. The number of individuals usually falls too, and generally falls faster, because organisms at higher levels tend also to be larger: a single hawk requires many snakes, each of which required many frogs, each of which required many grasshoppers. Representing this graphically gives the familiar pyramid of numbers and pyramid of biomass, broad at the base of producers and narrow at the apex. Two qualifications are worth stating. The pyramid of numbers can be inverted in particular cases, as when a single large tree supports thousands of insects, so the number pyramid is not universal even though the energy pyramid is. And the pattern explains why food chains are short: after four or five transfers the energy remaining is too small to support a further level of consumers at all. It also has a practical consequence, since a given area of land can feed many more people if they eat at the second trophic level as vegetarians than if they eat at the third as meat eaters.

items.stem: Assess the international response to ozone depletion as a model for dealing with environmental problems.
items.answer: The case has features that made action unusually achievable, and it is worth separating them from the general lesson. The scientific evidence was clear and dramatic: a measurable hole over Antarctica detected in 1985, a well-understood chemical mechanism by which chlorine from chlorofluorocarbons destroys ozone, and a specific and identifiable harm in increased ultraviolet radiation causing skin cancer, cataracts and crop damage. The number of substances involved was small and they were made by a limited number of companies, so regulation had a definite target. Technically feasible substitutes existed or could be developed, so compliance did not require anyone to abandon refrigeration. And the benefit of acting was shared by everyone, while no country could protect itself alone, which aligned national interests with collective action. The response, the Montreal Protocol of 1987, froze and then phased out production, and it is generally judged a success: the concentration of these chemicals in the atmosphere has fallen and the layer is slowly recovering. As a model it teaches three things: that clear science, a defined set of substances and available alternatives together make agreement possible, and that an international treaty with binding targets can work. But the limits of the model must be acknowledged. Problems such as climate change involve a substance produced by almost every human activity, with alternatives that are costly and disruptive, harms that are diffuse and delayed, and benefits of acting that are unevenly distributed. The ozone case therefore shows that international environmental action is possible, without showing that it is easy, and treating it as proof that any such problem can be solved the same way would be a misreading of why it worked.

Both A and R are true but R does not explain A

items.stem: State whether true or false: plastic is a biodegradable substance.
items.explanation: Micro-organisms cannot break most plastics down, so they persist for a very long time.

options.why: Most plastics resist microbial action and are therefore non-biodegradable.

items.stem: State whether true or false: every food chain begins with a producer.
items.explanation: Producers are the only entry point for energy into an ecosystem, so every chain starts with them.

items.explanation: Energy flow is unidirectional, since it is degraded to heat at every step and lost; matter is what cycles.

options.why: Energy flows one way and is lost as heat; only matter is recycled.

items.stem: Explain what an ecosystem is, name its components with examples, and distinguish natural from artificial ecosystems.
items.answer: An ecosystem is all the interacting organisms of an area together with the non-living surroundings in which they live, considered as a single functioning unit. Its abiotic component is the non-living part: air, water, soil, sunlight, temperature and minerals. Its biotic component is the living part, and this divides by function into three groups. Producers, the green plants and blue-green algae, capture sunlight and make their own food by photosynthesis, and they are the only route by which energy enters the system. Consumers cannot make their own food and take it from others; they are subdivided into herbivores such as the cow, carnivores such as the lion, omnivores such as human beings, and parasites such as the tapeworm. Decomposers, the bacteria and fungi, break down dead remains and wastes and release the nutrients back into the soil and air. Ecosystems are described as natural or artificial according to whether people manage them. Natural ecosystems, such as a forest, a lake, a grassland or an ocean, are self-sustaining, have high biodiversity and need no human intervention. Artificial ecosystems, such as a crop field, a garden, an aquarium or a park, are created and maintained by human beings, usually contain very few species, and depend on continual management through watering, weeding, adding fertiliser and controlling pests. A crop field left alone soon ceases to be a crop field, which is a good indication of the difference.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a food chain and a food web, and why the web is the more realistic description.
items.answer: A food chain is a single linear sequence in which each organism eats the one before it, for example grass, then grasshopper, then frog, then snake, then hawk. It is a useful simplification because it shows clearly how food and energy pass from level to level and how much is lost at each step. Its weakness is that it implies each organism has exactly one food source and exactly one predator, which is almost never the case. A food web is the network formed when the many food chains of an ecosystem are drawn together, so that each organism appears in as many chains as it actually belongs to. A grasshopper may be eaten by a frog, a bird or a lizard; a hawk may take a snake, a bird or a mouse; a mouse may eat seeds, insects or fruit. The web is the more realistic description for three reasons. It represents choice, so an organism whose usual food becomes scarce is shown as having alternatives. It represents the several roles an organism can occupy, since an omnivore may feed at the second trophic level on one occasion and the third on another, which a single chain cannot express. And it represents stability correctly. In a food chain, removing one species breaks the chain completely; in a web, the consumers above it can switch to other prey, so the system absorbs the loss. This is why ecosystems with high biodiversity are more resilient than simple ones, and it is the ecological argument for conserving species rather than only the ones we find useful.

items.stem: Trace the consequences of using a non-biodegradable pesticide on a crop, following it through the ecosystem.
items.answer: Begin with the spraying. Only a small part of what is sprayed reaches the target insects; the rest lands on the crop, on the soil and in the air. Rain then washes it from leaves and soil into streams, ponds and groundwater, so a chemical applied to one field is soon distributed across a much wider area, including water supplies. Because it is non-biodegradable, it is not broken down by micro-organisms and does not disappear over time. It now enters food chains at several points at once. Plankton in the water absorb it directly and, being unable to excrete it, retain it. Small fish eating large quantities of plankton accumulate the burden of all of them. Larger fish eating those accumulate again, and a fish-eating bird at the top of the chain may end with a concentration thousands of times that in the water. The same happens on land through the crop itself: the chemical is present in the grain or vegetable, so it passes to herbivores, to the animals that eat them, and to human beings, who as omnivores draw from the top of several chains at once. The consequences follow. Top predators are the worst affected, and since they are usually few in number and slow to breed, their populations can decline sharply, which was the fate of several birds of prey under DDT. Predatory insects and birds that had been controlling the original pest are killed alongside it, so the pest can return in greater numbers than before, and the farmer applies more pesticide, which deepens the problem. Resistant individuals among the pests survive and reproduce, so the pesticide loses its effectiveness over time. Soil organisms that maintain fertility are harmed. And the residue reaches human beings in food and water long after the spraying, by which time it is too widely dispersed to be recovered. The general lesson is that persistence in the environment is a hazard distinct from immediate toxicity, and this is why such chemicals have been restricted and why integrated methods of pest control, using resistant crop varieties, crop rotation and natural predators, are preferred.

items.stem: Assess what an individual can realistically do about waste and environmental damage, and how much difference it makes.
items.answer: An honest assessment must separate what an individual controls from what they do not. Several measures are genuinely within individual reach and have a direct effect. Segregating waste at source into biodegradable and non-biodegradable is perhaps the single most useful act, because every disposal method, composting, recycling, incineration and landfill, works far better on separated waste and very poorly on mixed waste; unsegregated waste makes recycling uneconomic. Composting kitchen and garden waste removes a large fraction of household waste from the collection system entirely and returns nutrients to the soil. Refusing single-use plastic bags and bottles reduces demand for material that will persist for centuries. Reusing containers, repairing rather than replacing, and buying less in the first place all reduce the waste created, and reduce is placed first among the three Rs precisely because waste never generated needs no handling. Saving electricity and water reduces the pollution associated with generating and treating them. Where individual action is weaker is in scale and in reach. A household's waste is a very small fraction of a city's, and most waste in an economy is generated in production and packaging rather than in the home, where the individual has no direct control. Many of the decisions that matter most, how electricity is generated, whether public transport exists, what packaging manufacturers are permitted to use, whether a city has a working recycling system, are collective and political rather than personal. The fair conclusion is therefore neither that individual action is decisive nor that it is pointless. Its value is partly direct, since segregation and reduction measurably lessen the burden, and partly indirect, since demand for alternatives makes them commercially viable and since people who act tend also to vote and campaign for systemic measures. What should be avoided is the belief that individual virtue is a substitute for regulation, because the largest sources of damage do not respond to it.

items.stem: If producers capture 10000 J of energy, how much is available to the primary consumers?
items.answer: By the ten percent law, about ten per cent of the energy passes to the next level, so the primary consumers receive about 10 per cent of 10000 J, which is 1000 J. The remaining 9000 J is used in respiration, lost as heat, passed out undigested or never eaten.

items.stem: In the chain grass, deer, lion, 20000 J is captured by the grass. Find the energy reaching the lion.
items.answer: Applying the ten percent law twice. The deer receives about 10 per cent of 20000 J, which is 2000 J. The lion receives about 10 per cent of that, which is 200 J. So only 200 J of the original 20000 J reaches the lion, that is one per cent. This compounding loss is why a third-level consumer needs a very large area of grassland to support it, and why chains are short.

items.stem: A pesticide is present in water at 0.002 ppm and in a fish-eating bird at 25 ppm. Find the magnification factor and comment on its significance.
items.answer: The magnification factor is the concentration in the bird divided by that in the water, that is 25 divided by 0.002, which is 12500. So the pesticide is twelve and a half thousand times more concentrated in the bird than in the water it ultimately came from. The significance is considerable. A concentration of 0.002 ppm in water would almost certainly be reported as safe by any direct measurement, and a person testing only the water would conclude there was no problem. Yet by the top of the food chain the concentration is at a level that can impair reproduction or kill. Two conclusions follow. Monitoring the environment alone is insufficient, and tissue concentrations in organisms at high trophic levels must be measured as well. And the hazard of such a chemical cannot be judged from its immediate toxicity at the concentrations used, since the danger arises from persistence and accumulation rather than from the dose applied.

items.stem: Match each organism in Column I with its role in Column II. Column I: (a) grass, (b) goat, (c) tiger, (d) fungus. Column II: (i) carnivore, (ii) decomposer, (iii) producer, (iv) herbivore.
items.answer: (a) grass - (iii) producer, making its own food. (b) goat - (iv) herbivore, a primary consumer. (c) tiger - (i) carnivore, a higher consumer. (d) fungus - (ii) decomposer, acting on dead matter.

items.stem: Match each waste in Column I with its category in Column II. Column I: (a) vegetable peel, (b) glass bottle, (c) cotton cloth, (d) polythene bag. Column II: (i) non-biodegradable, (ii) biodegradable, (iii) non-biodegradable, (iv) biodegradable.
items.answer: (a) vegetable peel - (ii) biodegradable, broken down quickly by micro-organisms. (b) glass bottle - (i) non-biodegradable, chemically inert. (c) cotton cloth - (iv) biodegradable, being cellulose. (d) polythene bag - (iii) non-biodegradable, persisting for centuries.

items.stem: Draw a labelled food web for a grassland and annotate it to show trophic levels and energy loss.
items.answer: At the base draw grass and small plants, and label them producers, first trophic level. Draw arrows upward from them to three separate primary consumers: a grasshopper, a mouse and a rabbit, labelling them herbivores, second trophic level; the arrows must point in the direction the food and energy travel, that is from the eaten to the eater. From the grasshopper draw arrows to a frog and to a small bird. From the mouse draw arrows to a snake, an owl and a hawk. From the rabbit draw an arrow to a hawk. Label the frog, bird and snake as secondary consumers, third trophic level. From the frog draw an arrow to the snake, and from the snake and the bird draw arrows to the hawk and the owl, labelling these top predators as tertiary consumers, fourth trophic level. Now add the decomposers: draw a box labelled bacteria and fungi to one side, with arrows into it from every organism in the web, and one arrow out of it back to the producers labelled nutrients returned to the soil. Annotate the diagram with three points. First, mark beside each upward arrow that only about ten per cent of the energy passes on, with the remainder lost mainly as heat, and note the consequence that the chain cannot extend much further. Second, mark that the mouse is eaten by three different predators and the hawk eats three different prey, annotating that these alternative routes are what make a web more stable than a single chain, since a consumer can switch if one prey becomes scarce. Third, mark that energy flows one way through the web and is lost, while matter returns through the decomposers, so the nutrient arrow forms a cycle and the energy arrows do not.

items.stem: Draw a labelled diagram showing the ozone layer, and annotate the process of its formation and depletion.
items.answer: Draw the curved surface of the Earth at the bottom of the page and above it two horizontal bands. Label the lower band troposphere, where weather occurs, and the upper band stratosphere, marking its height as roughly 15 to 50 kilometres. Within the stratosphere draw a shaded region and label it the ozone layer. From the top of the page draw arrows representing sunlight coming down, and split them into two kinds: visible light, drawn passing straight through the ozone layer to the surface, and ultraviolet radiation, drawn being absorbed and stopped within the shaded band. Label this absorption as the protective function, annotating that without it ultraviolet radiation would reach the surface and cause skin cancer, cataracts and damage to crops and plankton. Now annotate formation to one side of the layer: show ultraviolet light splitting an oxygen molecule into two free atoms, and each free atom combining with another oxygen molecule to give ozone with three atoms, noting that the process is continuous and maintains a steady amount. Annotate depletion on the other side: draw an arrow rising from the ground labelled chlorofluorocarbons from refrigerants and aerosols, and note that they are so stable that they reach the stratosphere unchanged. Show ultraviolet light breaking one apart to release a chlorine atom, and draw that atom destroying an ozone molecule, annotating that a single chlorine atom destroys many ozone molecules in a chain of reactions before it is removed, which is why small quantities have a large effect. Mark a thinned patch in the layer over one pole and label it the ozone hole, detected over Antarctica in 1985. Add a final annotation naming the Montreal Protocol of 1987, which froze and phased out these chemicals, and noting that recovery is slow because those already released persist for decades.

items.stem: Show from the ten percent law why food chains must be short and why a pyramid of biomass narrows upwards.
items.answer: Take the energy captured by the producers of an ecosystem as 100000 units, and apply the ten percent law at each transfer. The primary consumers receive about ten per cent, that is 10000 units. The secondary consumers receive ten per cent of that, that is 1000 units. The tertiary consumers receive 100 units, the next level 10 units and the next 1 unit. Now argue from these figures. The energy available to a trophic level sets an upper limit on the total living matter it can support, because every organism must obtain from its food both the material of its body and the energy to run its life processes. Since the energy falls by a factor of ten at every step, the total biomass that can be supported must fall by roughly the same factor, which is exactly why a diagram of biomass against trophic level is broad at the base and narrows sharply upwards into a pyramid. The shortness of chains follows from the same arithmetic. By the fifth or sixth level the energy remaining is a hundred-thousandth of what entered, which is too small to sustain a viable population of any organism: the individuals would be too few to find one another and breed, and a predator would have to search an impossibly large area for each meal. So the chain terminates, not because of any rule forbidding further levels but because there is nothing left to support one. Two checks confirm the reasoning. The pyramid of numbers can be inverted in special cases, as when one large tree supports thousands of insects, which shows that the argument depends on energy and biomass rather than on counting individuals. And the same arithmetic predicts a practical consequence that is observed: a given area of land feeds far more people when they eat at the second trophic level as vegetarians than at the third as meat eaters, since the intervening transfer discards ninety per cent of the energy.
